equivalents.note: The Tibetan fuses the refrain's musā pabaṇā into one compound, rlung byi, 'wind-mouse', much as Munidatta reads the mouse as the mind-wind, and its verb is negative (ma bsad, apparently 'not killed') where the Bengali says 'kill'.

The Tibetan has the mouse bore through a wall (rtsig pa 'bugs) where the Bengali has it dig holes, and its comment (cp.21.m3) makes the wall the fall into the bad destinies (ngan 'gro), where Munidatta takes gatī as gati, 'destiny'.

The Tibetan line has yid kyi chos, 'the mind's dharma', apparently reading amaṇa as manas, 'mind', and dhāṇa as a form of dharma (compare dhāma for dharma in song 5), where the Bengali seems to name something the mouse grazes on.

Where the Sanskrit calls the mind-mouse kāla because it destroys conventional bodhicitta, the Tibetan comment (which cites the line as nag po, 'black') calls it Rāhu (sgra gcan), destroyer of the moon of conventional bodhicitta, and its verse line 4a likewise has sgra gcan where the song has kalā.
In Mīnanātha's verse the Tibetan renders samādhika pāṭa as ting 'dzin sgo glegs can, 'having the door-panel of samādhi', taking pāṭa as a board or leaf (compare Sanskrit paṭṭa).

equivalents.wylie: phung po za bas dbye bas
equivalents.lemma: phung po za ba dbye ba
equivalents.note: The Tibetan does not treat the compound as the names of two meditations: phung po za bas dbye bas reads roughly 'by eating (or seizing) the heap and by dividing', with piṇḍa taken as phung po, 'heap, aggregate'.
The Tibetan renders the same phrase, svarūpam āha, as rang bzhin gsungs here but as ngo bo gsungs in cp.21.m4.

For pratyāropayatā the Tibetan has rkyen gyis brtags pa, 'imagined through conditions', apparently reading praty- as pratyaya, 'condition'; the verse quoted later in the segment renders mithyāropa with the usual log par sgro btags.
